story.headline: A global slide in stocks, after Nvidia's chief executive stepped down, pulled US yields lower and sent money into the yen and franc. Bets on a half-point Fed hike faded, and the dollar eased.

reads.policy: A quarter-point December Fed hike is still treated as all but certain, but bets on a bigger move faded as stocks slid. The European Central Bank, Bank of England and Bank of Japan are all expected to hike in December too. US rates still look set to rise further than most, though the gap stopped widening this week.
reads.growth: UK shoppers spent more than expected in October, partly by stocking up. Canadian sales rose on gasoline. A global stock slide raises worries that growth will slow, which would hit commodity currencies hardest.
reads.inflation: Inflation is still above target almost everywhere, which keeps most central banks leaning toward hikes. Japan's inflation came in a touch below forecast but stayed above the Bank of Japan's goal, so a December hike there still looks likely. In the US, war-driven costs are still feeding through, which is why the Fed is slow to treat softer growth as a reason to stop.
reads.risk: Nvidia's chief executive stepped down without warning, and stocks fell sharply in the US and Asia. Money moved into the yen, the franc and US government bonds. The Aussie stayed near its lows, as it usually does when stocks slide.
reads.tot: Gold fell to its lowest in more than a year, which keeps weighing on the Aussie. Oil is headed for a third weekly fall despite attacks in the Gulf, which takes support away from the Canadian dollar.
reads.positioning: The latest weekly figures show hedge funds leaning toward the dollar and the pound and against the euro, the kiwi and the Canadian dollar, with bets against the kiwi growing fastest. Big long-term investors take the other side on the euro, pound and Aussie. Where the two groups disagree, a surprise could set off a fast unwind.
reads.fiscal: France's debts, flagged by the European Central Bank as a risk, keep weighing on the euro. Record US government borrowing keeps long-term US borrowing costs near 5%, which weighs a little on trust in the dollar.

fed.summary: The Federal Reserve held rates on October 28 with two officials voting to hike. Almost all officials now expect more hikes, and neither soft US data nor a 2% fall in US stocks has shaken bets on a December move, which keeps the dollar near its highest since April 2025.
fed.priced: December: hike all but certain, with a half-point move a growing chance. More hikes expected next year.
fed.why: US inflation is running at about twice the Fed's 2% goal, and the prices factories pay are still rising. Chicago Fed President Austan Goolsbee says all options remain on the table.
fed.watch: The University of Michigan's survey of US inflation expectations Friday, November 20 at 9:00 AM CT, and whether the stock slide changes how officials talk. The decision is December 9.

boc.summary: The Bank of Canada raised rates to 2.50% in October and said more may be needed. October inflation held at 3.1% with core prices near 2%, so a December hike now looks less likely than not.
boc.priced: December: hold more likely, with a hike a bit under even odds.
boc.why: Energy is lifting headline inflation, but core prices are calm and the economy is shedding jobs, so the bank can afford to wait.
boc.watch: Oil prices, which fell sharply this week, and Canada's November jobs figures on December 4. The decision is December 9.

rbnz.summary: The Reserve Bank of New Zealand held at 2.75% in October in a narrow vote. Rising unemployment has made a December hike less certain, and the kiwi has fallen to its lowest since 2020.
rbnz.priced: December: hike possible but not fully expected.
rbnz.why: Inflation pressures argue for a hike, but unemployment at its highest since 2015 argues for waiting. Governor Anna Breman gave no clear signal on December in her latest speech.
rbnz.watch: The official election result on November 27 and the next dairy price auction. The decision is December 9.

ecb.summary: The European Central Bank held at 2.50% in October and a December hike is widely expected. Euro-area inflation is confirmed at 4.0%, but the euro sits just under $1.10 as US rates rise faster.
ecb.priced: December: hike widely expected, possibly the last for a while.
ecb.why: Euro-area inflation is about double the bank's goal and core prices are firming. Weak factories and France's debts, which the bank's stability report singled out, limit how far it can go.
ecb.watch: Euro-area business surveys for November next week. The decision is December 17.

boj.summary: The Bank of Japan holds at 1.25%, far below other major banks, and is expected to hike in December. Japan's October inflation came in a touch below forecast but stayed above the bank's 2% goal, which keeps that hike likely.
boj.why: Inflation has stayed above 2% for a second month, and the weak yen keeps pushing up import and food prices. The small summer contraction is the main reason to wait.
boj.watch: Any sign Japan steps in to buy yen near 160 per dollar, and Governor Kazuo Ueda's next comments. The decision is December 18.

rba.summary: The Reserve Bank of Australia raised rates to 4.85% on November 3, the highest among the major banks. Australia lost jobs in October and unemployment hit a five-year high, which supports the view that rates have peaked and has pushed the Aussie to an 11-month low.
rba.priced: December: a hold expected. Some bets on cuts in 2027 are building.
rba.why: Inflation is still too high for most of the board, but the job market is clearly weakening. That makes a further hike unlikely and puts the timing of a first cut in question.
rba.watch: Any comment from Governor Michele Bullock on the jobs figures, and gold prices. The decision is December 8.

boe.summary: The Bank of England raised Bank Rate to 4.00% on November 5 and said more may follow. UK shoppers spent more than expected in October, which supports a second hike in December, but the pound sits near its lowest this year as US rates rise faster.
boe.priced: December: a second hike more likely than not.
boe.why: High fuel costs from the Middle East conflict keep UK inflation near twice the bank's goal. Spending held up in October, although much of it was food stockpiling that may not last.
boe.watch: UK business surveys for November next week, after retail sales beat forecasts in October. The decision is December 17.

snb.summary: The Swiss National Bank holds its rate at zero and can sell francs if they get too strong. Low Swiss inflation means no hike is in sight.
snb.why: Swiss inflation is low, so the bank has no reason to raise rates and some room to cut if the franc climbs.
snb.watch: Any flare-up that sends money into the franc. The decision is December 10.

GBP.summary: The pound sits at the top of the board because UK interest rates are among the highest of the eight. Stronger UK shopping in October helps, but it is still near its lowest this year as heavy demand for dollars outweighs it.

AUD.summary: The Aussie sits second on the board, thanks to the highest interest rates among the major central banks. Australia's October job losses suggest those rates have peaked, and falling gold pushed the Aussie to an 11-month low.

USD.summary: The dollar sits third on the board. High and rising US interest rates support it, while large budget deficits weigh a little. It eased from its highest since April 2025 as a stock slide pulled US yields lower.

NZD.summary: The kiwi sits fourth, in the middle of the board. Firm prices for New Zealand's dairy exports help, but it stays close to its lowest since 2020 as the dollar holds firm.

EUR.summary: The euro sits fifth, just below the middle of the board. Cheaper oil helps the euro area, but France's debts and rates below most of the others hold it back. It sits just under $1.10 after touching its weakest in about 18 months this week.

CAD.summary: The Canadian dollar sits sixth, in the lower half of the board. Falling oil prices hurt Canada's exports, and recent Canadian data has mostly missed forecasts. It is at its weakest against the US dollar in more than a year.

JPY.summary: The yen sits second from the bottom because Japanese interest rates are far below the others. A global stock slide and a likely December Bank of Japan hike lifted it, pushing the dollar back from just under 160 yen.

CHF.summary: The franc sits at the bottom of the board. Swiss interest rates are the lowest of the eight and inflation is too low to need higher rates. A global stock slide sent safe-haven money into it, pulling the dollar off an 18-month high.
